title: Settle Debts in Fewest Payments
statement:
A group of friends shared costs on a trip. Each record [from, to, amount] in payments means person from paid amount on behalf of person to, so to now owes from that much.

A settlement transfer moves any amount from one person to another. Return the fewest transfers after which nobody owes anybody anything. Only each person's net balance matters, not who originally paid whom.

examples.why: Person 1 received 30 and paid 30, so their net is zero. A single transfer of 30 from 2 to 0 settles everything.
Nets: 0 is owed 6, 3 is owed 5; 1 owes 4, 2 owes 2, 4 owes 5. {3, 4} settle in one transfer and {0, 1, 2} in two. Pairing the biggest creditor with the biggest debtor first (0 with 4) needs 4.
The two records cancel out, so nobody owes anything.

hints: Collapse the records into one net balance per person. People with a zero balance can be ignored.
If k people have non-zero balances, k − 1 transfers always suffice. When can you do better? Look for groups whose balances add up to zero.

Each zero-sum group of size s needs only s − 1 transfers, so the answer is k minus the largest number of disjoint zero-sum groups. Backtracking finds it: settle person i fully against some later person of opposite sign and recurse.

explain.intuition:
First reduce the records to net balances. Someone owed 6 and owing 6 elsewhere is done, so only people with non-zero balances remain, say k of them. One transfer can always zero at least one person, so k − 1 transfers are enough. The saving comes from groups that cancel out on their own: a group of s people whose balances sum to zero needs only s − 1 transfers. So the answer is k − (number of zero-sum groups), and you want as many groups as possible.

Greedy matching of largest creditor with largest debtor ignores those groups and can lose, as the second example shows. With at most 12 people, search is fine. Backtracking takes the first unsettled person, moves their whole balance onto some later person of the opposite sign, and recurses. A bitmask DP gives the same result more predictably: for every subset, the most zero-sum groups it can be split into.
steps: Compute each person's net balance and keep only the non-zero ones in a list bal.
dfs(i): skip positions whose balance is already 0. If none are left, return 0.
For each later j with a balance of opposite sign, add bal[i] into bal[j], take 1 + dfs(i + 1), then undo.
Skip j values whose balance equals one you already tried at this level; they lead to the same subtree.
pitfalls: Answering with the number of non-zero balances minus one. That ignores groups that cancel among themselves.
Greedy largest-with-largest matching. It can split a group that would have settled cleanly.
Forgetting that transfers can be any amount: one person can absorb part of another's debt and pass the rest on.

complexity.time: O(k!) worst case for backtracking; O(2ᵏ · k) for the bitmask DP
complexity.space: O(k) for backtracking; O(2ᵏ) for the DP

solutions.title: Backtracking over net balances
solutions.idea: Settle the first non-zero person completely against each later person of opposite sign, recurse, and keep the minimum.

solutions.title: Bitmask DP: most zero-sum groups
solutions.idea: For every subset of non-zero people, store the most zero-sum groups it splits into. Adding one person to a subset adds a group exactly when the new subset sums to zero.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def fewestTransfers(self, payments: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        net = defaultdict(int)
        for a, b, x in payments:
            net[a] += x
            net[b] -= x
        bal = [v for v in net.values() if v != 0]
        k = len(bal)
        full = 1 << k
        total = [0] * full
        groups = [0] * full
        for mask in range(1, full):
            low = mask & -mask
            total[mask] = total[mask ^ low] + bal[low.bit_length() - 1]
            best = max(groups[mask ^ (1 << j)] for j in range(k) if mask >> j & 1)
            groups[mask] = best + (1 if total[mask] == 0 else 0)
        return k - groups[full - 1]

followups: Why is it safe to always settle the first non-zero person completely in the backtracking, instead of trying partial amounts?
Fifty people are involved. The exact answer is NP-hard; what quick heuristic would you ship in a bill-splitting app?
